item.title: New Fund Closes at $1.9 Billion as Office Hangover Sidelines Rivals
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Town Lane Management closes second fund at $1.9 billion, betting fresh capital and no legacy office exposure gives it edge over rivals.

The post New Fund Closes at $1.9 Billion as Office Hangover Sidelines Rivals appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Town Lane Management closed its second real estate fund at $1.9 billion, exceeding its target by more than 25%. Founder Tyler Henritze, who spent nearly two decades at Blackstone before launching the firm with his sister Parker Morse in 2023, began marketing the vehicle in May. Commitments came from endowments, foundations, family offices and pension funds. Individual investments will range from $50 million to $300 million.

Henritze points to the firm’s lack of legacy holdings as a competitive advantage while older funds work through portfolios weighed down by office exposure and elevated interest rates. Commercial real estate values remain roughly 25% below their prior peak, according to JPMorgan Chase. Town Lane’s first fund, which raised $1.25 billion, backed senior housing, retail and small-business industrial properties. The firm also entered a joint venture with PowerHouse Data Centers to acquire land in North Carolina for a data center shell with power infrastructure.

Henritze left Blackstone in 2023, where he most recently served as head of strategic investments for real estate in the Americas and helped execute the acquisition of QTS Realty Trust. Town Lane has hired from TPG, Starwood Capital Group, Coatue Management and Blackstone. An advisory group includes former Blackstone executives Michael Nash and William Stein, and Guy Metcalfe, who led Morgan Stanley’s real estate investment banking business for more than two decades.

item.title: Industrial Outdoor Storage Spans 1.4 Million Acres and Still Is Not Enough
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
AI demand is reshaping a market that may not have the right space

The post Industrial Outdoor Storage Spans 1.4 Million Acres and Still Is Not Enough appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
2 hr 11 min agoOct. 26, 2026 4:16 pm

Every gigawatt of data center capacity requires roughly 100,000 truckloads of steel, concrete, generators, and equipment, according to DAT Freight and Analytics. Much of that material needs somewhere to wait before installation. Industrial outdoor storage (IOS), a largely overlooked category of gravel and asphalt yards used to store equipment, materials, and vehicles, has become one of the better-performing corners of commercial real estate. The AI buildout is adding demand for staging space to a market that already has very little of it.

Newmark estimates the sector spans about 1.4 million acres nationally, though the investable share is far smaller. Alterra IOS has put the total value above $1 trillion, with most of that land municipally or government-owned, leaving roughly $300 billion held by small local owners and operating businesses. Vacancy runs around 4 percent, compared with roughly 7 percent for traditional industrial, while annual inventory growth remains below 2 percent.

That scarcity shows up in rents. CBRE puts national rent growth at 32 percent since 2021, while Alterra IOS data shows rents up more than 110 percent since 2020 across the top eight port-adjacent markets, including Houston, Savannah, and Norfolk. Part of the pricing power comes from how little the rent matters to the tenant: yard costs are a rounding error against total data center development budgets.

Capital has arrived accordingly. Brookfield agreed this year to acquire Peakstone Realty Trust for $1.2 billion, J.P. Morgan Asset Management partnered with Zenith IOS on roughly 100 properties across 33 markets, and a Starwood Property Trust venture lent $672 million against a portfolio in August. Catalyst Investment Partners has assembled $1.4 billion over six years in Northern Virginia and Atlanta, financed partly by Blackstone.

But the investment thesis has a supply-side problem. Entitling new outdoor storage is close to impossible in many jurisdictions, where these yards often face opposition over noise, appearance, and relatively low tax revenue per acre. Meanwhile, data center development is consuming some of the existing supply. In Manassas, Virginia, more than 200 acres of outdoor storage will be replaced by data centers, representing over 20 percent of the local supply. The same development boom driving demand for staging space is helping eliminate the land that could provide it.

The scale of hyperscale development complicates the thesis. IOS aggregators typically assemble infill parcels of two to fifteen acres from regional operators and retiring owners, properties well suited to trucking companies and equipment rental businesses. Large data center projects introduce a different set of requirements, particularly when contractors need substantial laydown areas close to construction sites. Cushman & Wakefield put the average data center land purchase in 2024 at 224 acres, up 144 percent from 2022, while a gigawatt campus generally needs 500 to 1,500 acres. Crusoe’s Stargate site in Abilene covers roughly 1,100 acres for 1.2 gigawatts, and Meta’s Hyperion campus in Louisiana spans about 2,250 acres under construction.

A project of that size cannot necessarily solve its staging needs by leasing a dozen scattered eight-acre yards. Contractors may need multiple smaller properties for specific logistics, but large projects can also create demand for substantial, contiguous areas near the site. Developers increasingly secure adjacent parcels alongside substation easements and land reserved for future phases. Parts of the IOS sector have begun shifting toward hubs of 50 acres or more, a different product with different entitlement hurdles. The transition is complicated by an existing inventory in which roughly 60 percent of properties were developed before 2000, with many still unpaved or lacking the drainage, lighting, and security institutional users expect.

The near-term numbers reflect a genuine shortage, but the demand underneath them is less uniform than the rent growth suggests. Yards serving ports and last-mile fleets face structural constraints that predate AI and will outlast it. Yards serving a specific data center campus may be scarce only for the duration of construction, after which the contractor leaves. Upgrading older properties and assembling larger sites also takes capital, time, and potentially new entitlements.

The key question is whether aggregators holding infill portfolios can capture the hyperscale demand bidding up rents, or whether much of that demand will flow to larger, contiguous sites the existing investment model was never designed to assemble. Industrial outdoor storage may be benefiting from the AI boom, but not every yard is positioned to benefit equally.

The post Industrial Outdoor Storage Spans 1.4 Million Acres and Still Is Not Enough appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Major Brokerages Form Alliance to Counter Private Listing Networks
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Four major brokerages launch Open Real Estate, a free data-sharing platform designed to counter private listing networks and expand access to property information.

The post Major Brokerages Form Alliance to Counter Private Listing Networks appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
AGNT Inc., HomeServices of America, Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group announced the formation of Open Real Estate, a national data-sharing platform that will allow participating brokerages to distribute property listings across multiple listing services, real estate portals and other authorized recipients. Brown Harris Stevens, Lamacchia Realty, Samson Properties and Windermere Real Estate joined as participating brokers. Participation is free for brokerages, and the founders have invited other firms to join. The platform is designed to work alongside existing MLSs rather than replace them.

The initiative arrives as Compass challenges MLS rules that limit private listing marketing, creating a widening divide over who controls listing data. Compass allows sellers to market homes within its brokerage network before making them widely available, a strategy it says gives sellers more control. Open Real Estate positions itself as a counterweight to that approach, focused on sharing listing data rather than restricting access. The founding companies argue that limiting listing information reduces buyer access and seller exposure, potentially increasing time on market and affecting property value.

The platform is built around four principles: expanding buyer access to housing information, helping sellers make informed marketing decisions, protecting listing data integrity and promoting fair competition. Participating brokerages and agents will be able to enter listings into the shared technology platform, which will then distribute property information to MLSs and portals. The founders say the infrastructure will establish clear governance and data ownership rules while making it easier for industry participants to exchange property information.

The alliance reflects broader industry tension over the fragmentation of property listing information as more homes are marketed through private networks. For agents, a national data-sharing platform could provide broader access to inventory and reduce reliance on individual brokerage networks. The founding companies emphasized in an open letter that sellers should understand how their properties are being marketed and the potential trade-offs of different marketing strategies, stating that success should be determined by those who create the most value rather than those who control the most information.

item.title: Five Decisions That Make or Break a Portfolio-Wide EV Charging Rollout
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Learn how Olen Properties scales EV charging across a diverse portfolio by balancing tenant demand, electrical capacity, costs, and future growth.

The post Five Decisions That Make or Break a Portfolio-Wide EV Charging Rollout appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Ask an asset manager why their older buildings still don’t have EV chargers, and the answer usually has little to do with demand. The project dies in the budget meeting, after the cost of a new electrical panel gets loaded onto four Level 2 ports and the payback runs longer than anyone can justify.

Olen Properties has found ways around that problem across one of the more varied portfolios in commercial real estate. The Newport Beach firm, founded in 1974, owns more than 8 million square feet of office, flex, warehouse and R&D space and roughly 17,000 multifamily units in eight states. Some of those buildings went up decades ago and others in the last few years, and their electrical systems vary accordingly.

Olen worked with SWTCH Energy to figure out where chargers should go and how to pay for them. Taylor Curtis, Olen’s director of asset management, described a process that other owners with mixed portfolios could adapt.

Tenants are asking

CBRE found that roughly 70 percent of prime US office buildings offer charging, compared with only about 5 percent of multifamily buildings. In NMHC and Grace Hill survey data, renter interest in EV charging rose from 27 percent to 34 percent over two years.

At Olen, the request came up through property management. “Property managers were telling us how important it is to compete in the market,” Curtis said. “It is becoming pretty critical for certain markets now.”

It also comes up during lease talks. “Some of our capital decisions get made at the point of leasing. They can often come from a tenant renewal negotiation where they are pushing for this,” Curtis said. “It is much cheaper than an empty building.” A charger installation that keeps a tenant from leaving is easy to justify against months of vacancy, even if the chargers barely cover their own electricity costs.

Start with who will use them

Olen began by counting cars. The team audited how many EVs were parked at each property, a large number in Southern California, and then looked at how far tenants and residents commuted. Long commutes were a good indicator of who needed to charge during the day.

“Initially, we just looked at demand, which properties would use the chargers the most,” Curtis said. “Buildings where people had to commute a long way, for example.”

Electrical assessments came later. Working in that order meant Olen spent its engineering budget on properties where chargers would actually get used.

Look for the easy electrical wins

“The biggest challenge in doing this to older properties is finding a way to provide enough capacity with the existing electrical grid,” Curtis said. Some of Olen’s parking garages have only enough power for their lights. Others have capacity to spare.

Olen looked for properties where it could add two to four chargers without upgrading electrical service, since that is where retrofit costs start to climb. Level 2 ports typically cost $5,000 to $15,000 installed at multifamily properties, and retrofit work can run three to five times what the same installation would cost during construction. A few of Olen’s projects cost only a few thousand dollars.

Load management helps stretch the power that’s already there. Software that caps how much each property’s chargers can draw lets more ports share the same electrical service, which can delay or avoid a panel upgrade.

When a new panel couldn’t be avoided, Olen only went ahead at properties where it expected to add more chargers later.

Two budgets instead of one

The most useful part of Olen’s approach is how it handles the math. Rather than judge each site as one investment, the company splits it in two.

“We look at the electrical upgrades as a long-term cost, with a 20-year payback or thereabouts,” Curtis said. “Then we looked at the return on the initial hardware costs and wanted to see it have about a 5 to 7 year payback.”

Panels, conduit and service upgrades will outlast several generations of chargers, so Olen treats them like other long-term building improvements. The chargers are treated as an amenity with a much shorter payback window. Lump the two together and the electrical work can sink a project even when the chargers would pay for themselves.

Curtis compares charging to adding a gym. It’s there to attract and keep tenants, so the company charges just to break even and keep costs down for tenants. “We are long-term owners, so in that perspective, it makes the decisions a lot easier,” he said.

Software that works with any charger

Olen’s properties don’t all need the same thing from a charging system. “What you need in an office parking lot is different from an apartment building,” Curtis said. Some garages don’t need network connectivity. At some properties, tenants pay for charging directly, while at others the property pays and recovers the cost.

Many charging vendors want to control the whole system. “There are so many contracts where the vendors want to be in control,” Curtis said. Olen wanted a single dashboard for its apartment and commercial properties that would work with whatever hardware was installed. “We didn’t want to put all of our eggs into one hardware basket.”

SWTCH’s platform gave Olen that. The team runs Wallbox chargers, takes reservations, sets pricing and tracks energy costs from one place, and its own staff manages the system. “It allowed us to disentangle the software from the hardware,” Curtis said.

For a long-term owner, that flexibility counts. Chargers will be replaced over the life of a building. With the software kept separate, Olen can change hardware without much difficulty.

Plan for more demand than you expect

“There is a lot more demand for these than we initially forecasted,” Curtis said. “The second you put them in, people start changing their habits, and we see a lot more EVs getting charged at the parking lots. Once you put them in, you can’t take them out, because people will start to expect them.”

That affects how many chargers to install. A property that puts in the bare minimum may find them full within a year, and by then residents expect to be able to charge. Running extra conduit and leaving panel capacity for a second phase costs much less while the walls are already open.

Less upkeep than expected

“These systems are fairly hands off,” Curtis said. Olen reviews them once a year to keep pricing in line with electricity rates. Staff needed some training on the network side, though Curtis said most problems are fixed by resetting the connection.

Learn more about how SWTCH works with owners across property types and charger brands at swtchenergy.com/parking.

The post Five Decisions That Make or Break a Portfolio-Wide EV Charging Rollout appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: AI Was Supposed to Reduce Office Demand. So Far It Has Done the Opposite.
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
AI office demand is surging as record funding drives tech firms to lease larger spaces in San Francisco, New York, Silicon Valley, and beyond.

The post AI Was Supposed to Reduce Office Demand. So Far It Has Done the Opposite. appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The capital flowing into artificial intelligence has reached a scale that makes previous technology cycles look modest. CB Insights put US private AI funding at $206 billion in the first quarter of 2026 alone, approaching what the entire prior year produced. That money is going into model development, data center capacity, chips, and the engineering talent required to build any of it.

Hiring engineers means putting them somewhere, and the companies doing the hiring have reached a conclusion about where that should be. Nick Romito, co-founder and CEO of VTS, has watched the posture of tech tenants reverse over the past few years. “Post COVID the tech companies were pushing back against the return to the office,” he said. “Now they are driving the return, a lot of companies are even bringing people in on Saturdays because they know they can’t win this race to innovate if they are remote.”

VTS tracks live office requirements across 17 markets, and its data shows national AI office demand up 85 percent year over year, with growth of 179 percent across the largest AI hubs. AI companies now account for 46 percent of the square footage tech firms are actively pursuing. The requirements themselves are larger than typical tech deals, averaging 37,000 square feet against 27,000 for tech overall.

That demand is not spread evenly. San Francisco, Silicon Valley, and New York together hold roughly two-thirds of all active AI square footage, and a single San Francisco submarket covering SoMa and Mission Bay accounts for a quarter of national AI demand on its own. San Francisco’s 81 active AI requirements average 62,000 square feet, more than double the average tech requirement across the markets VTS follows.

The composition differs by market. San Francisco skews toward foundation model labs, while New York draws application-layer companies and AI infrastructure firms selling into its financial, legal, and media base. New York recently moved past Silicon Valley into second place for active AI demand, with 2.79 million square feet against Silicon Valley’s 2.78 million, and it now has more requirements over 50,000 square feet than Silicon Valley does.

Secondary markets are starting to register. Seattle posted the fastest growth of any market VTS tracks at 390 percent year over year, and Northern Virginia grew 169 percent on defense and government technology work. Los Angeles and Boston are the only markets moving the other direction.

What makes the current cycle different is how quickly it has compressed. After the financial crisis, San Francisco anchored tech demand in 2010, New York followed by 2013, and Seattle entered by 2016. This time those markets activated close to simultaneously.

The broader expectation about AI and office space ran in the opposite direction. If AI automates enough knowledge work, companies need fewer people, and fewer people need less space. That logic shaped a good deal of commentary about where office demand was headed, and it has not yet shown up in leasing data.

Ryan Masiello, co-founder and chief strategy officer at VTS, thinks the reason has to do with the limits of distributed work for the kind of problem-solving these companies are doing. “Unless you are a company that started as a remote company, it is really hard, if not impossible, to have the same productivity over Slack,” he said.

The broader market numbers point the same way. New York became the strongest office market in the country in the second quarter, supported by a 113 percent year-over-year increase in technology demand. San Francisco ranked second with trailing twelve-month tech demand up 161 percent. Excluding San Francisco, which was coming off a record first quarter, technology demand rose 19 percent quarter over quarter.

There is an early signal that the effect is spreading beyond AI tenants themselves. Professional services requirement velocity in San Francisco is up 33 percent year over year, which follows the pattern from prior cycles where tech leasing led and other industries followed into the same submarkets.

Whether that holds depends on things nobody can forecast with confidence. AI funding could contract the way tech funding did in 2022, when companies that had hired ahead of revenue cut staff quickly. The productivity effects that were supposed to reduce headcount may simply be arriving on a longer timeline than the leasing data covers. And the concentration in a handful of submarkets means a landlord underwriting to metro averages is reading a market that does not exist at their property.

For now, the companies building this technology are leasing more space than their predecessors did at the same stage, and they are doing it while telling their employees to come in on weekends.

The post AI Was Supposed to Reduce Office Demand. So Far It Has Done the Opposite. appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Instant City Races to Build Tax Base From Scratch
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
San Tan Valley incorporated as Arizona's largest new town with 104,000 residents, zero staff, and borrowed funds. Now it's chasing commercial tenants.

The post Instant City Races to Build Tax Base From Scratch appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
San Tan Valley incorporated in September 2025 as an instant town of 104,000 residents in Pinal County, Arizona — the largest new incorporation in state history. Starting with zero staff, no infrastructure, and no access to tax revenue, the town borrowed operating funds from neighboring Queen Creek for ten months while building out basic municipal functions. Brent Billingsley, hired as the first employee in December 2025, led a 15-person team to operational independence by July 1, 2026. The town had to navigate federal and state bureaucracy to unlock state-shared revenue, which remains its primary funding source alongside a new transaction privilege tax that took effect October 1.

San Tan Valley leases office space from Pinal County and contracts with the county sheriff’s office and Rural Metro Fire for emergency services. Residents will vote November 3 to raise the state-imposed spending cap from $91 million to $850 million, a ceiling the town expects to grow into over time. Neighboring Queen Creek, with a smaller population, operates under a $650 million limit. First-year revenue reached roughly $51 million. Financial priorities hinge on a 10-year general plan now in development, with goals including land acquisition, a town hall, parks, and road expansion.

Mayor Daren Schnepf and Billingsley both aim to diversify beyond the town’s bedroom-community reputation by attracting industrial and commercial tenants. An estimated 600 businesses currently operate in San Tan Valley, serving 37,000 to 39,491 housing units. A battery storage site has been approved, and town leaders are touring data centers to educate the Council on potential energy infrastructure projects. A 3,238-acre state-owned parcel bounded by Hash Knife Draw Road, Bella Vista Road, Hunt Highway, and Gantzel Road is envisioned as a walkable downtown core where developers can pitch mixed-use plans to the state through the town.

Economic development leaders from Queen Creek, Casa Grande, and Maricopa cautioned San Tan Valley to manage expectations and treat growth as a marathon. Doreen Cott, Queen Creek’s economic development director, noted that projects often take years to materialize. The advice comes as San Tan Valley seeks to recapture sales tax leaking to neighboring cities and build a commercial base capable of supporting its population. Recent openings of a Winco Foods and In-N-Out Burger mark early commercial traction in a town that had no billing system or computers a year ago.

Go Behind the Curtains of Arizona's Newest City

item.title: Buyer Sues Broker Over $650 Administrative Fee in Post-Commission Settlement Era
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A Pennsylvania buyer sued Keller Williams Elite over a $650 closing fee, alleging breach of fiduciary duty and seeking class action status for similar charges.

The post Buyer Sues Broker Over $650 Administrative Fee in Post-Commission Settlement Era appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Gregory Deivert filed suit against Keller Williams Elite in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, alleging the brokerage charged him a $650 fee at closing in October 2023 without proper disclosure or corresponding service. Deivert claims the fee breached fiduciary duty and violated Pennsylvania consumer protection law. The complaint states the charge first appeared on the closing statement, a point at which buyers rarely walk away from a transaction. Deivert is seeking class action status for all buyers who paid similar flat fees to the brokerage beyond commissions already paid by sellers.

Keller Williams Elite allegedly instructed agents to describe the fee as mandatory and tied to administrative costs such as document preparation. Deivert’s complaint argues that document preparation is a legal obligation of brokers under Pennsylvania law, not a separate billable service. Other Keller Williams franchises across the country have reportedly charged similar fees under names including “Additional Broker Commission” and “Compliance Fee.” Keller Williams Elite did not respond to requests for comment.

A parallel case in Florida ended in voluntary dismissal two months after filing. Jeff and Melissa Efron had challenged a $475 transaction fee from Compass, also seeking class action status. Industry estimates suggest consumers pay up to $2 billion annually in brokerage transaction fees. Deivert has demanded a jury trial and seeks both damages and a permanent injunction barring the $650 charge.

Pennsylvania Lawsuit Targets $650 ‘broker Fee’ at Keller Williams Franchise

item.title: The Case For Building a Real Estate Tech Stack From the Inside Out
item.dc:creator: Thano Lambrinos
item.description:
Multifamily operators need an independent proptech strategy to control costs, avoid vendor lock-in and build flexible, AI-ready technology stacks.

The post The Case For Building a Real Estate Tech Stack From the Inside Out appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
AI has triggered an unprecedented proliferation of technology solutions. New platforms emerge constantly, each promising to solve operational complexity, reduce cost or unlock competitive advantage. 

The pace of innovation and the pressure to adopt and modernize means that the current corporate real estate system often rewards inertia in the short term. Shiny new offerings often outrun the industry’s ability to evaluate what it is really buying. As a result, too many operators are allowing their strategic technology direction to be steered by vendors selling “solutions,” rather than the people within their businesses who are most familiar with the operational problems that actually need solving.

What makes this pattern so persistent is that the broader ecosystem tends to reinforce it. Consultants recommend familiar products, installers deploy what they know, then service providers maintain existing systems and software platforms for property management, leasing, energy management and more. Refresh cycles bring the same conversations back around. It’s not that anyone in this chain is acting in bad faith; it’s that the incentive structure doesn’t naturally reward asking harder questions about whether a better approach exists.

We’ve seen this play out across the industry with several high-profile proptech companies that raised significant capital, achieve notable valuations and then shifted direction (or went out of business), leaving operators with stranded technology investments and the cost and disruption of replacing infrastructure or software platforms they’d only recently deployed. The pattern isn’t unique to any one company. It reflects a structural gap between how vendors grow and what operators really need.

This pattern is not unique to multifamily either. Across all real estate asset classes, organizations without strong internal technical capabilities consistently cede strategic control to vendors. Over time, this produces rigidity, inflated costs and infrastructure and platforms that are more challenging to evolve as needs change over time.

The operators who will lead the industry long term are those who resist that dynamic. Multifamily is at an inflection point. The challenge is no longer access to tools. It is building the internal capability to evaluate solutions independently, align them to organizational objectives and make decisions grounded in a portfolio’s reality, rather than riding the latest wave of market momentum.

Building a more independent posture requires real investment: in people, in process and in the willingness to take positions that may diverge from prevailing industry practice. That’s not easy, but it’s well worth it in the long run.

Constructing a strong talent foundation is a critical first step. Sometimes the right move is actually looking outside of the multifamily industry, finding engineers and technologists with backgrounds in data centers, hospitals, manufacturing or other sectors where operational complexity is high and the consequences of poor technology management are tangible. These are professionals who have seen what good looks like in other contexts, and who are well-equipped to hold vendor relationships to a high standard, recognizing when a proposed “solution” falls short.

From there, strategy should be developed independently of what the market is selling. That means clearly defining what the organization is seeking to accomplish across its stakeholders – operations teams, residents and investors – before approaching a market that is oversaturated with options. Real estate companies need to tell the market what they need, rather than the other way around.

When building or evaluating a technology stack, the principles that tend to produce durable results are modularity, openness and long-term flexibility. Prioritize open APIs, operator-owned data, infrastructure with long useful lifecycles and systems that integrate cleanly and can evolve without forcing a full rebuild every few years. These are not novel ideas, but they are consistently underweighted when technology decisions are driven by market momentum rather than internal strategy.

The opportunities that follow from this approach are meaningful. Operators who own their technology relationships have more flexibility over cost structure and functionality than those locked into enterprise platforms. Infrastructure decisions — such as deploying passive optical networks rather than defaulting to traditional active copper architectures — can create substantial long term operating advantages that compound over time. Additionally, we find that automation practices more commonly associated with commercial offices can translate more directly into residential environments than the industry has historically assumed.

None of this requires proprietary technology breakthroughs. It requires the right people, a clear strategy and the discipline to evaluate technology decisions from the inside out.

It has never been more important to be in control of a tech stack than in the wake of unprecedented AI disruption. Operators are making significant commitments to AI vendors at a moment when the landscape is still evolving and business models are still being tested. This choice is popular now, but it’s riskier than it might appear on the surface.

After all, popularity in the market and fit for every portfolio’s strategy are two very different things. The most important discipline in proptech right now is knowing the difference.

The post The Case For Building a Real Estate Tech Stack From the Inside Out appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Six Regional MLSs File Joint Lawsuit to Block Compass Policy Challenge
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Six regional MLSs sue Compass in New York federal court seeking to uphold listing cooperation rules and block threatened litigation over pre-marketing policies.

The post Six Regional MLSs File Joint Lawsuit to Block Compass Policy Challenge appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Arizona Regional MLS, BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS, and REcolorado filed a joint lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 21 in the Southern District of New York. The six organizations, which represent more than 120,000 real estate professionals, seek a declaratory judgment that their cooperation rules comply with federal and state antitrust laws. The suit also requests a permanent injunction barring Compass from suing any of the six MLSs over their listing submission and pre-marketing policies. The action follows demand letters Compass sent to MLSs in September threatening litigation against any organization that fines agents who violate listing rules.

Compass sent letters demanding that MLSs allow brokers to market listings publicly without submitting them to the cooperative database. The brokerage argues homesellers should control how their property is marketed without agents facing fines. The six MLSs counter that Compass wants to access MLS data for its buyer clients while withholding its own listings, a practice they characterize as free riding that undermines the cooperative model. Greg Skidmore, representing the plaintiffs, said the rules ensure transparency and broad access to timely listing information. Compass pointed to several MLSs across 12 states that currently permit public marketing without MLS submission.

The complaint alleges Compass aims to use its inventory as leverage to drive smaller brokerages out of business, reducing competition and consumer choice. California Regional MLS filed a separate lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 5 after receiving a similar demand letter. Compass countersued CRMLS less than a week later, alleging the MLS enforces competition-blocking rules through fines, suspensions, and expulsions. Rocket Companies, which partnered with Compass earlier this year, co-signed an open letter in March accusing certain MLSs of working against member agents. Other large MLSs including Unlock MLS and OneKey MLS have issued public responses defending their listing policies.

ARMLS, 5 Other MLSs Sue Compass Over Pressure Campaign

item.title: Rent Payment Platforms Face Legal Challenge Over Undisclosed Transaction Fees
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Baltimore sues property manager and rent payment platforms over undisclosed transaction fees charged to low-income tenants through electronic payment systems.

The post Rent Payment Platforms Face Legal Challenge Over Undisclosed Transaction Fees appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore’s city solicitor filed suit against Pennrose Management Company, RentCafe, and Yardi Systems, alleging they charged tenants undisclosed fees for electronic rent payments that violate Maryland consumer protection law. Tenants at nine Pennrose-operated low-income housing developments faced annual service fees of $300 to $420 when paying by credit or debit card through the RentCafe platform, according to the complaint filed in Baltimore Circuit Court. Pennrose switched to mandatory electronic payments in 2024, eliminating in-person rent collection. A free automatic payment option exists but requires a bank account, which many low-income tenants lack.

Rents at Pennrose properties range from $869 for one-bedroom units to $1,654 for four-bedroom apartments, housing primarily older adults, people with disabilities, and residents on fixed incomes. The lawsuit argues tenants received no additional services in exchange for the fees but risked eviction if they refused to pay. City Solicitor Ebony Thompson said renters should not have to navigate unclear charges to understand their payment obligations. Representatives for all three defendants did not respond to requests for comment.

Baltimore renter households paying more than they can afford for rent and utilities account for roughly 40 percent of the city’s rental market, with very low-income renters facing the most acute burden. A 2024 lawsuit filed by Baltimore resident Rodney Deaver against his landlord over similar charges resulted in a judgment exceeding $250,000, roughly 800 times what the defendants acknowledged owing. Baltimore Circuit Judge Catherine Chen justified that award based on the inconvenience and dismissiveness Deaver encountered. Organizations in neighboring Howard County, Maryland have begun warning tenants about mandatory fees for trash valet services, parking permits, and other charges residents cannot decline.
